cards.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64

depth.text: someone found a **serious flaw** in Java that can let attackers **run code remotely**
The decoder mishandles **malformed padding**, causing a **write past its output array**. It needs x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, and every target requires a **bespoke exploit profile**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some think bespoke attack chains and network constraints make mass exploitation unlikely; others expect many affected hosts and a long tail of high-value targets to remain at risk.

comments.text: From the section on performing heap grooming over the network ("Remote Heap Feng Shui"): > The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For…

Super impressive work by Calif as usual. The exploit conditions are very specific but there are still going to be a lot of hosts impacted. We at Semgrep published some free detection scripts here: https://github.com/semgrep/detection-scripts/tree/main/CVE-2... They look for these five conditions: * HotSpot VM: any OpenJDK build, Oracle JDK, or GraalVM JDK. Only HotSpot generates the stub. OpenJ9…

What’s that old Chinese proverb? “May you live in interesting times”? It feels like we’re living in interesting times. How long will it take for a bad actor to seriously compromise critical infrastructure? My bet is within six months. The upside is that it’ll force legacy institutions and organizations with sub-par security to get good at security and modernize their legacy stacks. That, or get…

Unconfirmed, but people on Twitter suggest this vulnerability has to do with the AVX512 implementation of Base64 decoding, and so this vulnerability can be worked around by running Java with the -XX:UseAVX=2 flag. ( https://x.com/sean_a_cassidy/status/2122791344573976817 )

cards.title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed

depth.text: someone used **Io’s eclipses** to show that **light takes time to travel**

He noticed **Io’s eclipse timings shifted**: they were later than expected when Earth moved away from Jupiter, and earlier when it moved toward it. In 1676, he predicted Io would emerge **ten minutes later than expected**; he was right. His speed estimate was **about 25 per cent too low** by modern standards.

cards.title: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%

depth.text: Google's **AI answers** are taking clicks from websites, leaving publishers with **fewer visits** from search

In a randomized experiment with US desktop Chrome users, searches that would show an Overview averaged **0.37 clicks** to outside websites when the group saw them, versus **0.62** when Overviews were hidden; the authors report a **39.8% reduction**. It’s a working paper, not yet peer reviewed.

cards.title: jQuery 4.1.0

depth.text: a familiar web library got a **new release** with **selector and XML fixes**

jQuery 4.1.0 adds a **`responseURL` field** to `jqXHR`, supports **form-associated custom elements**, and fixes **ReDoS in identifier matching**. It also drops `getElementsBy{Tag,Class}Name` in favor of `querySelectorAll`.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say jQuery still suits small site enhancements and value its event model; others prefer vanilla JS or modern frameworks and see little reason to use it.

comments.text: The composability of jQuery has been an inspiration for the way I design my own frameworks and tools. One thing I still regularly use jQuery for, though, that's rarely mentioned, is its event model. You can put a listener on any object, not just things in the DOM. Any data object can trigger an event. This is incredibly powerful for isolating logic from DOM elements and events. A frequent use…
Although jQuery isn't very relevant these days, I still find its pattern of chaining a sequence of methods on a set chosen by a selector to be a beautiful example of going with a language's features.

I'm a tad surprised jQuery still exists, though it's kinda neat it does. Always interesting to see historical projects with less and less modern day relevance get continued like this. And while most of the use cases for jQuery have long since died out with things like classList, querySelector, etc, I do feel there's probably value in a framework that focuses on minor enhancements to a site rather…

I remember how painful it was to deal with IE/Netscape. Event handlers, etc... jQuery made so many lives easier. It’s quite an achievement, and I can stretch to say that JavaScript development might not be here today without it!
I'm actually surprised (in a good way) that it's still maintained, and it still helps half of the internet to function

cards.title: Solid 2.0

depth.text: Solid's **new release** is stable, with **async data** and clearer warnings built into its UI framework

Computations can return a Promise or async iterator, letting downstream code handle **async work** and race conditions automatically. **Server functions** support RPC calls and persistent connections, while development builds flag **reactive mistakes** with their location and a fix.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say agent-focused diagnostics help people writing code by hand too; others dismiss the AI framing or argue that agents make frameworks unnecessary.

comments.text: What's amusing and/or interesting is that the stuff under "Built to Be Written by Agents" also would make it easier to write by hand, I imagine. It's just better debug diagnostics; nothing really to do with agentic development specifically. Maybe that's just marketing, but it's really intriguing how human best practices are also agent best practices; how, maybe, we've reached a point where even…

Remix originally pitched itself as solving the 'middle' layer between frontend and backend. Closing the gap. It never quite managed to do so imo. Solid's solution here is beautiful. The server RPC and 'live' and 'broadcast' are seamless, and feel much more natural to use than liveview or htmx/datastar imo.
A gist I wrote about my experience migrating from Solid 1.0 to Solid 2.0 (RC) a couple of months ago: https://gist.github.com/FlameWolf/7b3be7acb06775f02ea4a57297...

Congrats to Ryan and the team. I never got deep enough into front-end to understand the nuance of these things but I still occasionally tuned into his Friday streams just to listen. You can tell he cares about this subject deeply and I enjoy listening to passionate people talk about their craft.
There are still not many component libraries for Solid. But if I needed to build something from scratch, I would definitely try Solid. It just feels like the right way React should be.

cards.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

depth.text: a Harvard study found **AI agents** brought more code, but **finished work stayed flat** as **reviews slowed**

Across 718 firms, the authors found engineers added **about 30 percent more code**, while **finished work did not measurably rise**; time from pull-request submission to merge took **49 percent longer**. The working paper has no indication of completed peer review, and the study examined software, not legal work.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say human review is still the painful bottleneck; others say agents and changed review practices can handle the code, leaving specs, testing, or prioritization as the real pinch point.

comments.text: All I do all day is review ai written code. my own or teammates. I really do not enjoy it.

A lot of this university research on AI feels dated. This is something we all faced months ago. Many times they're also reaching conclusions using obsolete models, etc. Feels like things move too fast for traditional research cycles to catch up to AI dev

The problem is that when nobody writes code or feels ownership over it anymore, nobody will be qualified to or really interested in doing the code reviews. The way forward could involve dropping code reviews altogether. You could argue that the useful pingpong between coder and reviewers has been replaced by the similar pingpong between the prompter and the agent.

This has been obvious for a while. The big speed up comes from not having to understand the code - e.g. not doing thorough human review. Personally I find that super hard, because whenever I review AI code I find many things that could have been a lot simpler or more readable. But whether I like it or not, I think we are heading more and more towards just trusting the machine.

cards.title: Do Repeat Yourself

depth.text: someone says teams should **keep their tools** and **repeat some work** instead of forcing one stack

In the bank example, the platform team picks Go, React, and Kubernetes for everyone, and a requested chart feature gets **deprioritised**. The proposed **service-oriented architecture** instead standardizes **RESTful APIs** and their documentation, while leaving API implementation to each team.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say copying is cheaper than a bad shared abstraction; others want shared UI standards and gradual migration to avoid a disjointed product.

comments.text: Sometimes syntactic duplication can give you a hint to underlying semantic duplication. But it's no more than a hint. DRY doesn't mean don't repeat a similar looking block of code, it means try to structure your code so that each element of the design has a single representation. There's no shortcut to good design where no thinking is required, much as a lot of people seem to wish there were.
Or as the go proverb goes "a little copying is better than a little dependency" ( https://go-proverbs.github.io/ )

We are exactly where the hypothetical bank is. Our large outer company gobbled up nine or ten smaller companies with disparate stacks (PHP, Haskell, C#, a few others). After a couple years of integrating through shared APIs, new management is trying to force us all into a single platform - Go and Node+React. We have thousands of years of combined experience in our various technologies and we are…

My company has a script to set up a repo in an expected pattern. The first thing you have to do is disable a bunch of logging that no one uses, as that can cripple the performance of your app. Then you have to go update a bunch of dependencies with security problems. Then you have to fix their git hooks. Which is to say, standard does not imply good. A lot of times companies just standardize…
reminds me of WET: Write Everything Twice. Instead of immediately jumping to DRY, actually write out the two similar tools, then see what actually makes sense to combine into a shared dependency.

glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.Base64: A way to represent data as ordinary text characters, even when the data itself is not text.
glossary.heap: Memory a program can request as it runs, useful when it doesn’t know in advance how much space its data will need.
glossary.AVX-512 VBMI: Special processor instructions that let some computers handle many bytes at once.
glossary.CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a scale people use to rate how serious a security flaw is.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.DNS resolver: Domain Name System resolver: a service that looks up a website's name and tells your device where to find it.
glossary.rightsholder: A person or organization that owns rights to something, such as copyrighted material.
glossary.ISP: Internet Service Provider: a company that connects people to the internet.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.splinternet: A split-up Internet where countries or regions have different rules or access.
glossary.exploitation: Using a software flaw to make a computer do something its makers did not intend.
glossary.reverse engineering: Figuring out how a program works by examining the program itself.
glossary.CTF: Capture the Flag: a security game where players solve challenges to find a hidden answer.
glossary.zero-day: A security flaw attackers can use before its maker has a fix.
glossary.arbitration: A way to settle a dispute with a neutral decision-maker instead of a judge or jury.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
glossary.SSO: Single Sign-On: a way to use one sign-in for several work services.
glossary.eclipse: When one object disappears behind another or into its shadow; Io disappears into Jupiter’s shadow.
glossary.finite speed: A speed that is limited, so light takes time to get from one place to another instead of arriving instantly.
glossary.stellar aberration: Stars seem to shift slightly across the sky during the year because Earth moves while their light travels.
glossary.AI Overview: A Google-made summary placed above ordinary search results, with links to the pages it used.
glossary.SEO: Search engine optimization: making changes to a webpage so it is more likely to appear in search results.
glossary.GEO: Generative Engine Optimization: work to help content show up in answers from AI search tools.
glossary.CTR: Click-through rate: the share of people who see a result and then click it.
glossary.referring domain: A website that links to another website.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.jqXHR: jQuery's object for a web request, which holds information about the request and its response.
glossary.ReDoS: Regular expression denial of service: a flaw where crafted text can make matching code take an extremely long time.
glossary.querySelectorAll: A browser method that finds all page elements matching a selector.
glossary.form-associated custom elements: Custom HTML elements that can take part in a form, such as sending a value when the form is submitted.
glossary.XML: Extensible Markup Language: a way to label pieces of information so computers can store and exchange them.
glossary.fine-grained reactivity: A way for an app to update only the parts affected when data changes, rather than refreshing everything.
glossary.reactive graph: A map of how pieces of app data depend on each other, so the app knows what needs updating when something changes.
glossary.Promise: A value that will arrive later, like the result of a request to fetch data.
glossary.async iterator: A sequence of values that arrive over time rather than all at once.
glossary.server functions: Functions called from an app that run on a server instead of on the user's device.
glossary.RPC: Remote Procedure Call: a way for one program to ask another program to do something directly.
glossary.Server Sent Events: A way for a server to keep sending updates over one open connection.
glossary.ONNX Runtime: A tool that lets software run machine-learning models.
glossary.evals: Short tests used to check how well a model handles tasks you care about.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.telemetry: Information a program sends back about how it is being used or whether it is working properly.

glossary.warm leads: People who may be interested in buying because they already have a connection to the seller.

glossary.working paper: A research paper shared while it is still being developed, rather than a finished, peer-reviewed journal article.
glossary.DOM: Document Object Model: the browser's list of the pieces that make up a webpage.
glossary.XSS: Cross-site scripting: A flaw that can make a website run instructions supplied by someone visiting it.
glossary.CSRF: Cross-site request forgery: tricking a signed-in browser into sending a request the user didn’t intend.
glossary.event loop: The browser’s turn-taking system for handling code, clicks, and other events.
glossary.rendering pipeline: The steps a browser takes to turn a page’s code into what appears on screen.
glossary.accessibility tree: A version of a webpage’s content that tools like screen readers use to explain it to people.
glossary.canvas: A webpage area where code can draw pictures or other visuals.
glossary.WebAssembly: A way to run compiled programs inside a web browser.
glossary.TLD: Top-Level Domain: the ending of a web address, like .com.
glossary.layout engine: The part of a browser that decides where text and other things go on a page.
glossary.SOA: Service-Oriented Architecture: a way to build software from separate parts that interact through agreed rules.
glossary.REST: A common way for one app to send requests to another app over a network.
glossary.DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself: a guideline to avoid writing the same code in several places.
glossary.Kubernetes: A system for running and managing software containers across computers.
